title: Fulcrum Grid - GPU sourcing & cost model sync
next_steps: Jordan to send initial pricing band and reserved capacity options
Priya to run quick perf estimate for their 512-token baseline and share a simple benchmark spreadsheet
Samir to share current instance utilization CSV and expected Q4 forecast
action_items: Jordan: email pricing & SGX/marketplace pass-through note by 2025-09-05
Samir: share utilization export and SLA expectations by 2025-09-07
header: Date: 2025-09-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Maya Chen (Redwood) / Samir Patel, Leah Gomez, Tom Anders, Alex Ruiz (Fulcrum Grid)
summary: Introductory partner discovery focused on Fulcrum Grid's GPU sourcing needs for an upcoming ML inference marketplace. Discussed hybrid procurement, pricing sensitivity, reserved vs burst capacity, regional constraints, compliance and pass-through billing. Agreed next steps: pricing spreadsheet, perf estimate, and sharing utilization data for pilot sizing.
topics: current procurement model and pain points
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we really appreciate you making time. quick roll call?
[00:12] Samir (Fulcrum): Yep Samir here, Leah, Tom and Alex on my side. thanks Jordan.
[00:18] Jordan: Awesome. Priya and Maya are with me from Redwood. we're going to mostly listen, ask clarifying Qs, and then Priya will do a short perf framing. sound good?
[00:29] Leah: yup that's perfect, we just want to make sure this call stays tactical. procurement side will be quiet except for price questions.
[00:35] Priya (Redwood SE): cool. Samir, maybe you can frame top priorities? cost, latency, compliance? what are you optimizing for?
[00:45] Samir: Right now it's mostly cost predictability and time-to-market. Fulcrum is building an ML inference marketplace for third-party models — we need predictable unit economics to set vendor margins. latency matters - we target sub-200ms P95 for short chat prompts (<=512 tokens) but that can bend if cost is prohibitive.
[01:10] Alex: also regional constraints: customers in eu-west and ap-southeast want data locality. and some financial customers require dedicated tenancy.
[01:22] Jordan: ok great — that lines up with common patterns. are you currently buying GPUs via cloud marketplace or direct instances?
[01:29] Tom: a mix. we have some reserved capacity on major clouds but most of the new marketplace partners would rather buy through a reseller/marketplace channel. the challenge: marketplaces add fees and sometimes opaque pricing.
[01:42] Priya: totally - pass-through fees and reseller margins can change per-provider. one approach is Redwood Dedicated or Private for committed capacity and then hosted API for bursts or low-touch customers.
[01:53] Samir: can you say more about dedicated vs hosted? what are the real levers that change cost & latency?
[02:00] Priya: Sure. dedicated means reserved GPU pools that you control — predictable throughput and lower unit price per token but you pay for unused capacity unless autoscaling is tuned. hosted is pay-as-you-go, lower operational lift but variable latency and higher unit price. there are middle grounds: committed capacity + burst to hosted, or reserved with autoscaling/burst credits.
[02:21] Leah: from procurement perspective, committed spend is ok if we can forecast utilization. our finance team wants a 12-month runway or a pilot that transitions.
[02:30] Maya (Redwood): quick interjection — we also have a quantization and model variant recommendation flow. small models + int8/4 quant can reduce cost by 2x-4x for many workloads while keeping quality. might be useful for margin math.
[02:43] Alex: interesting — do you operate quantized variants in the same routing layer? how hard is that to manage?
[02:49] Priya: we can expose routing policies: e.g. route to quantized variant for low-cost tier, or to full fp16 for premium customers. KV cache and prefix caching also helps with repeated prompts.
[02:59] Tom: do you have any restrictions on model licensing or model types in dedicated/private? some partners want to run proprietary 3rd-party models.
[03:08] Jordan: our private option supports customer-managed images and you can load models; licensing and legal IP are customer-managed. Redwood provides the runtime and orchestration. for hosted catalog models we have curated models and usage terms.
[03:22] Samir: okay. let's talk baseline numbers — for a 512-token P95 sub-200ms target, what does the per-token unit cost look like for dedicated vs hosted?
[03:32] Priya: rough ballpark, varies a lot by GPU type. on A100-like hardware, dedicated with good utilization might get to X cents per 1k tokens; hosted tends to be ~1.5-2x that. i'll put concrete bands in the spreadsheet.
[03:45] Leah: when you say "get to X cents" — procurement needs a formula we can plug into forecasts. can you share the assumptions?
[03:52] Priya: yes assumptions: hardware type, batch size, average prompt length, kv cache hit rate, tokenization overhead, nvlink/PCIe efficiency for multi-GPU. we'll include both conservative and aggressive assumptions.
[04:08] Jordan: quick ops question — Fulcrum's marketplace partners, will they expect single-tenant VPC per partner? or can you map partner accounts into a shared pool?
[04:19] Samir: ideally shared pool with tenant isolation at the orchestration layer, but larger partners want dedicated tenancy. it's a mixture.
[04:27] Maya: Redwood Private supports per-tenant VPC peering and customer-managed keys via KMS. audit logs and RBAC are included for private.
[04:36] Tom: any SOC2/ISO attestation for hosted? some of our banking partners will require that.
[04:41] Jordan: our hosted control plane is SOC2 Type II — we can share the security pack. Private has options for on-prem or VPC with customer-managed keys.
[04:50] Leah: perfect, please add the SOC2 doc to the pack.
[04:53] Jordan: noted.
[04:55] [05:00] Priya: moving to procurement mechanics — marketplaces: sometimes vendors require the reseller to charge extra license line items or per-hour instance fees. Fulcrum wants to understand pass-through vs take-rate. Samir?
[05:12] Samir: yes. take-rate is crucial — we plan to keep a 20-30% margin but if the marketplace fee is 15% on top of vendor GPU fee, margins compress quickly. we need transparency on all components.
[05:26] Priya: we can show itemized components: base GPU unit cost, Redwood service fee, optional monitoring/retention add-ons, and any region egress or marketplace fees. some partners negotiate flat reseller discounts.
[05:38] Alex: Curious about bursting to hosted — is that seamless from a billing perspective? we'd rather not have complex passthrough invoices from multiple clouds.
[05:46] Jordan: Redwood can consolidate billing under a single invoice for Redwood Dedicated and Hosted usage; for third-party cloud marketplace purchases you may still get separate bills depending on partner arrangement. we do have examples where partners let us invoice the customer and then settle with the provider.
[05:59] Samir: we need an example contract appendix showing marketplace pass-through language — do you have template?
[06:06] Jordan: yes, we'll share a redlineable clause.
[06:09] [06:15] Priya: switching to performance — any model families you're planning to host? LLama-ish, GPT-like, or vendor models?
[06:23] Samir: a mix. some partners will bring Llama variants and smaller quantized models for cost-sensitive customers; others want to offer proprietary large models that require fp16 on higher-end GPUs.
[06:35] Priya: okay that lets us size GPU types. small quantized variants favor lower-memory GPUs and high batch multiplexing, big proprietary models need A100/4090-class with higher memory and NVLink for sharded models.
[06:49] Tom: do you do automatic kernel selection and tuning per model? we don't want to manage that complexity.
[06:55] Priya: yes, the runtime picks optimized kernels based on model arch, sequence length distribution, and hardware. sometimes we need small compile steps for custom kernels which we can automate during onboarding.
[07:08] Alex: any constraints around preemptible / spot instances? potentially lower cost but higher variability.
[07:14] Jordan: you can use spot/preemptible for non-latency-critical tiers, but we recommend that critical partners get reserved or dedicated pools with fallback policies.
[07:25] Samir: fallback — does that mean automatic model routing to another region or to hosted variants?
[07:30] Maya: yes, fallback policies can route to a compatible quantized variant, a hosted pool, or a different region depending on your policy.
[07:39] Leah: ok. procurement will want a list of supported regions and any extra network egress charges.
[07:45] Jordan: we'll provide a region matrix with egress and typical latency bands.
[07:50] [08:00] Priya: quick note on observability — Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency, traces and error rates so you can attribute cost to partner or tenant. that usually helps marketplaces with billing reconciliation.
[08:14] Alex: good. can we custom tag partners for billing?
[08:17] Priya: yes tags at the token/request level are supported.
[08:20] Tom: what about data retention? some partners want log retention for 90 days, others 1 year. any constraints?
[08:26] Jordan: retention is configurable. storage costs are additional but we can create tiers. also Private allows you to keep logs within VPC.
[08:34] Samir: let's discuss pilot sizing — we expect about 300K tokens/day initially across partners with spikes to 1M. thinking a 3-month pilot. what size GPU pool do you recommend?
[08:45] Priya: rough first-cut: if mix is 70% small-quantized and 30% larger models, you can start with a few mid-range GPUs (e.g., 4x 80GB equivalents) for control plane and then buy reserve credits for additional burst. but i need your utilization export to give exact numbers.
[09:02] Samir: i'll share the CSV.
[09:05] Leah: procurement question — do you support monthly committed vs annual? finance prefers annual discount, but operations want flexibility.
[09:13] Jordan: both options. committed annual gives best price per token; monthly committed is possible at slightly higher rate. we can model both.
[09:22] [09:30] Priya: Perf note: caching has outsized impact for marketplace workloads where many requests are similar — prefix caching and KV can reduce token compute significantly. even a 20% cache hit can change the economics materially.
[09:45] Alex: hmm interesting, many marketplace requests are repeated templated prompts. this could help a lot.
[09:51] Tom: any vendor lock-in concerns with caching? if we adopt Redwood routing, could we move off later?
[09:57] Maya: we aim to keep routing config portable; caches are based on request keys you control. model artifacts can be exported, though exact kernel optimizations may be vendor-specific.
[10:08] [10:15] Samir: what about model onboarding timeline? if a partner brings a new model, how long until it's available?
[10:21] Priya: small models often are available same-day with our runtime. larger sharded models may take 24-72 hours for sharding and kernel tuning; private/on-prem has a slightly longer lead for provisioning.
[10:33] Leah: procurement wants SLAs — what's your P95 latency SLA on Dedicated?
[10:38] Jordan: Dedicated SLA is 99.9% with target P95 depending on model class, often we commit to specific latency bands in the contract.
[10:46] Samir: are there penalties or credits if SLA misses?
[10:49] Jordan: yes typical SLA credits apply — we'll share the standard SOW language.
[10:54] [11:00] Priya: competitive question — you mentioned marketplace partners may resell other infra like Lambda. does Fulcrum already have relationships?
[11:07] Samir: we've done spot buys on Lambda and are exploring a multi-provider strategy.
[11:12] Priya: good — Redwood can route based on policy so you could use low-cost providers for non-critical tiers and high-performance nodes for premium tiers.
[11:22] Alex: curious about an example cost model — can you sketch a sample monthly P&L for a single partner with expected 100k tokens/day?
[11:30] Priya: sure — high-level: raw GPU cost, Redwood service fee, storage/retention, monitoring, marketplace take-rate, and partner margin. we'll send a sample template.
[11:41] Leah: please surface any hidden fees like egress, model licensing, or support add-ons.
[11:47] Jordan: will do.
[11:50] [12:00] Samir: security quick: are keys customer-managed in Private?
[12:04] Maya: yes KMS/HSM integrations supported. for hosted we store keys in Redwood vault but offer customer-managed key options for encryption at rest.
[12:14] Tom: audit logs and per-token tracing — is that available in Hosted?
[12:18] Jordan: yes, but retention windows differ; Private gives full control.
[12:22] [12:30] Priya: any hard dates for Q4 launch?
[12:34] Samir: we'd like pilot in Oct with GA in Nov if pilot goes well — some partners require November availability.
[12:40] Leah: procurement needs a 30-day cancellation clause for the pilot — is that feasible?
[12:44] Jordan: yes standard pilot terms include 30-day opt-out; we'll include that in the contract draft.
[12:51] [13:00] Priya: ok final quick technical checklist we'll deliver: benchmark estimate for 512-token baseline, region latency matrix, pilot sizing, itemized pricing bands, SOC2 + security pack, and sample contract pass-through clause.
[13:14] Samir: sounds good. any blockers from Redwood side?
[13:18] Jordan: none. we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[13:22] Alex: one last thing — do you have telemetry for model quality regressions and can we tie that into partner SLAs?
[13:29] Priya: yes we have evals and quality monitoring that can trigger rollbacks and alerts; we can include quality SLOs in the contract.
[13:37] Leah: thanks everyone. procurement will review the pricing when it arrives.
[13:42] Jordan: great. recap of next steps — Jordan sends pricing & legal clause, Priya sends perf spreadsheet, Samir shares utilization CSV. we'll aim to reconvene after artifacts to size the pilot.
[13:55] Tom: okay thanks, talk soon.
[14:00] [END]
